#3. The Pope cancels a visit to Assisi as a medical precaution, two weeks before his South American tour

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Pope Leo XIV has cancelled a visit planned for Tuesday, October 27, to Assisi, in central Italy, after his doctors advised against helicopter travel so soon after the lung surgery he underwent on October 13. It is the first engagement on his schedule to be called off since the operation, two weeks before the start of his tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

According to a medical bulletin released by the Vatican on Friday, a follow-up chest X-ray “confirmed his optimal post-operative recovery”. “However, given the short time that has elapsed since surgery, the attending physicians considered it appropriate to advise against the helicopter flight planned for October 27 as a precautionary measure,” it added.

In Assisi, the Pope was due to take part in a peace gathering marking the 40th anniversary of the World Day of Prayer for Peace convened by John Paul II. He will send a message to the organisers and participants.

Leo XIV, 71, underwent surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, where he was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma. On Wednesday, the Vatican said the tumour was localised and that he will not need further treatment. On Sunday, in his first appearance before the faithful since the operation, the Pope said he would resume his activities “gradually”.

The Vatican has announced no changes to the South American tour, scheduled from November 6 to 17, which will begin in Uruguay, from the 6th to the 8th, and continue in Argentina, until the 11th, and in Peru.

#4. Burnham tells Trump of the “economic consequences” of Argentina’s Falklands measures

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham set out to US President Donald Trump on Friday “the economic consequences that Argentina’s coercive measures have for the United Kingdom and the United States”, in a phone call focused on the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, according to a Downing Street statement quoted by the EFE news agency. Burnham reiterated the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources.

The call came a day after US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau acknowledged in Buenos Aires that Washington is closely watching the impact Argentina’s National Sovereignty Defence bill could have on its companies. The bill, still stalled in the Chamber of Deputies, extends sanctions to affiliates, shareholders, financiers and suppliers of companies operating in the islands. Trump has said in recent weeks that the US position of neutrality on sovereignty over the archipelago is under review.

The same day, Burnham spoke with Chilean President José Antonio Kast, to whom he raised “the UK’s interest in ensuring that Falkland Islanders retain the ability to exercise their right to self-determination”, according to Downing Street. The two agreed on the need to work together to modernise their defence capabilities and that there are “untapped trade opportunities” between their countries. Kast reiterated Chile’s support for Argentina’s sovereignty claim during a state visit to Buenos Aires in April, while his government described the new commercial route between Punta Arenas and Stanley in September as “a business between private parties”.

Argentina launched sanctions proceedings in September against dozens of people and companies linked to Sea Lion, operated by Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, and asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order a halt to the project. The tribunal will hold its hearing on November 10 and 11 in Hamburg. The United Kingdom has announced measures to protect its companies from Argentine sanctions and maintains that the islanders’ decision to remain British, expressed by 99.8% of voters in the 2013 referendum, must be respected.

'it is a well-established practice, accepted as law that title over natural resources is to follow that over territory: accordingly, the sovereign subject enjoys the exclusive right to dispose of the natural wealth of the area which it exercises sovereignty.' (UN Stockholm Declaration 1972, Principle 21 & UN Rio Declaration 1992, Principle 2,Declarations on the Human Environment).

#7. Paraguay’s president travels to Washington and will meet the CIA director

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña travelled to Washington on Wednesday for a brief visit that includes a meeting with US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) Director John Ratcliffe and a keynote address at the annual gala of the Inter-American Dialogue think tank.

Peña will be away until Friday, accompanied by Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez and the head of the presidential Civil Cabinet, Javier Giménez, according to the Senate. The president confirmed he will be “meeting the CIA director”, without giving further details. He will also take up an invitation from George Washington University, and the Inter-American Dialogue gala will be held at the headquarters of the Organization of American States.

Before leaving, Peña accompanied US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in the Alto Paraná department on the final day of his official visit to Paraguay. The two toured a new military unit created to fight terrorism and organised crime in the Triple Frontier area with Brazil and Argentina, and the binational Itaipú dam. Landau is now continuing his tour in Buenos Aires.

Peña has declared himself an ally of the White House on foreign policy. In January he signed in Davos, together with Argentine President Javier Milei, the founding charter of the Board of Peace promoted by Donald Trump to oversee the Gaza peace plan, and Paraguay is a member of the Shield of the Americas, the regional security alliance promoted by Washington.

#9. Bolsonaro apologises twice to Lula in a calmer final debate as polls show a dead heat

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro apologised twice to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva during the last televised debate before Sunday’s runoff in Brazil, held on Friday night on TV Globo, which was more measured in tone than the first. The candidates arrived level: the latest Datafolha poll, published on Thursday, gives each 50% of valid votes.

The first apology came when Lula asked why he had voted against extending maternity leave as a state deputy in Rio de Janeiro. “It was a mistake,” Bolsonaro replied. “Today, after having children, I would vote completely differently.” Lula retorted: “When you had the chance to vote in favour, you didn’t.” The second came after the senator called the president “nine fingers”, a nickname referring to the finger he lost in a workplace accident as a metalworker. “I will not allow a militiaman to call me nine fingers,” Lula replied, contrasting his working-class background with his rival’s. Lula also asked him about having once referred to Bolsa Família as “Bolsa Fodder”.

Argentine President Javier Milei featured again. Lula compared his rival’s proposals with those of the Argentine government, and Bolsonaro turned the argument around: “In Argentina, the left governed for 20 years and destroyed the country. Milei began his government with 200% inflation.”

Bolsonaro, who won the first round with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%, focused on the cost of living and public debt. He promised to cut taxes, raise the minimum wage and pensions above inflation and not to privatise oil company Petrobras or Banco do Brasil, and challenged Lula for the vote in the northeast, his main stronghold: “I will be the most northeastern carioca you have ever seen.” Lula defended his investment in infrastructure and in that region, accused his rival of not knowing the country and recalled the oxygen shortage in Manaus hospitals during the pandemic.

The debate was held under new rules barring candidates from entering each other’s space, requested by Lula’s campaign after the first encounter. On Saturday, candidates may take part in events but can no longer ask for votes.

#11. Inter-American Court hears case over the April 11, 2002 killings in Caracas

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held this week in San José, Costa Rica, the first public hearing in the case over the killings of April 11, 2002 in Caracas, when an opposition march came under gunfire near the Miraflores Palace. Nineteen people died and dozens were wounded that day, in the run-up to the coup that removed then-president Hugo Chávez from power for two days.

The case, known as Trujillo et al. v. Venezuela, was brought before the inter-American system that same year by lawyers Alfredo Romero and Gonzalo Himiob of the NGO Foro Penal. The Inter-American Commission referred it to the Court on July 9, 2024, after concluding that the Venezuelan state had violated the rights to life, personal integrity, assembly, and judicial guarantees and protection, and had not shown that the use of lethal force was legitimate, necessary or proportionate. The Court has yet to rule.

Testifying before the court, journalist Delvalle Canelón, who witnessed the shooting from a rooftop and was a witness at the trial held in Venezuela, said she had been threatened during that process by two of the men who fired from the Llaguno bridge and who were later acquitted. “There has been no investigation in Venezuela into these events. There is total impunity that persists to this day,” Romero said. Mohamed Merhi, father of Jesús Capote, an 18-year-old shot in the head, said impunity “is the result of a system that has protected those responsible”.

The only people convicted over the events were Metropolitan Police officers, released this year, and police commissioner Iván Simonovis, who escaped house arrest in 2019 and lives in exile. Although Venezuela denounced the American Convention on Human Rights in 2013, the Court retains jurisdiction over events that occurred before that date.

The parties have until November 13 to submit their final written arguments, which may include alleged victims left out of the initial file and the request for reparations.

#14. Eight in ten Argentines barely make it or fall short by the end of the month, survey finds

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Some 45% of Argentines just about reach the end of the month and 34% fail to cover their expenses, according to a survey by consultancy Brain Network carried out in September, which describes a picture of financial stress, rising debt and little capacity to save. Among those who had trouble paying, 40% use their credit card to cover shortfalls.

The study classifies respondents into three groups. The “Jugglers”, 57%, keep up with payments through frequent adjustments and a fragile balance; the “Up to date”, 22%, are more stable; and the “Overwhelmed”, 21%, have insufficient income and recurring arrears. People over 50 predominate in the first group, and those aged 30 to 39 among those facing the most severe difficulties.

Some 79% of respondents have a credit card. Besides using it to cover shortfalls, those who had trouble paying resorted to cutting spending, 31%; borrowing from family or friends, 23%; delaying payments, 17%; and taking out loans, 16%. In the past six months, 60% of those with bank debts and 65% of those owing digital finance platforms had difficulty paying. Among the “Overwhelmed” with problems, 21% took out a new loan to cover another debt.

“The market is not in default, it is juggling,” said Lionel Holzman of Brain Network, who recommended that lenders offer refinancing before the situation worsens. Some 45% of those in arrears say they have not received any such offer.

President Javier Milei recently challenged the idea that people cannot make ends meet: “If they really run out of money on the 20th, how do they live ten days without eating or drinking?” he said in Neuquén. According to the survey, 44% believe their situation will improve next year, 36% that it will stay the same and 20% that it will worsen.

#16. Uruguay signs a US$5.7 billion data centre investment with Spain’s Solaria

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi on Wednesday signed an agreement with Spanish company Solaria Energía y Medio Ambiente to develop a data centre campus of up to 500 megawatts with its own solar generation, a US$5.7 billion investment the government described as the largest in the country’s history. The opposition has demanded explanations about the company’s financial capacity and the jobs the project will create.

The project, under a free-trade-zone regime, will allocate US$5.5 billion to the data centres and US$200 million to a 350-megawatt solar plant to supply the complex. It will be built in two phases: the first, with 200 megawatts of data centres in Canelones and the solar plant in Florida; the second, with a further 300 megawatts in San José. Construction would begin in 2027. The planned 500 megawatts are equivalent to almost a tenth of Uruguay’s installed power capacity.

In a filing with Spain’s securities regulator, Solaria said the memorandum provides for a power purchase agreement of up to 40 years with state utility UTE, and that the company will develop and operate the free zone and its connection to the transmission grid. The campus, initially geared to cloud services, will use low-water cooling systems. The listed company has operated in Uruguay for almost a decade. Orsi called the agreement “a signal from Uruguay to the world” and credited state policies maintained by successive governments.

According to the government, the project will create 3,100 jobs during construction and 1,500 permanent posts. The opposition National Party said it will summon Industry Minister Fernanda Cardona to Parliament. “There is not a single private analyst, of the 10 I consulted, who tells me Solaria is in a position to take on a US$5.7 billion investment,” said Senator Sebastián Da Silva, who also questioned the employment figures.

UTE’s opposition board member, Darío Castiglioni, has requested the agreement’s documentation and the technical and legal reports supporting it. The utility’s vice president, Roberto Bentancor, said confidentiality had been maintained because Solaria had “other offers” that could have led it to drop Uruguay, and pledged to provide the information.

#17. Kast and Paz open the way in La Paz to normalising Chile-Bolivia relations

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Chilean President José Antonio Kast and his Bolivian counterpart Rodrigo Paz pledged on Friday in La Paz to move towards normalising diplomatic relations “at the highest level”, broken off since 1978, during a visit the Chilean government described as historic as the first official bilateral visit by a Chilean president to Bolivia in more than seven decades. The two governments signed economic integration and border security agreements, although they did not announce the restoration of embassies.

“President Paz, today we stop turning our backs on each other. We did not come just for a gesture, we came to begin making history,” Kast said after the bilateral meetings. Paz replied that the two countries have “historical differences” and that the claim to sea access is enshrined in Bolivia’s Constitution, “but Bolivia understands that this history cannot hold back its development. Problems of the past must be resolved.” Kast invited Paz on a state visit to Chile in 2027.

Ministers from both countries signed agreements on mining integration, electricity interconnection, bi-oceanic corridors, border security and the migration status of Bolivians living in Chile. They also discussed reviving the Arica-La Paz railway, provided for in the 1904 treaty between Bolivia and Chile, 24-hour operation at the Tambo Quemado-Chungará border crossing and the fight against smuggling. According to the Oruro customs post, more than 76% of Bolivia’s foreign trade passes through the Chilean ports of Arica and Iquique.

Bolivia’s claim to sovereign access to the sea, which it lost at the International Court of Justice in 2018, was not on the agenda. “We are not going to renounce our historical claim, but it is also clear that we have to address a fundamental agenda,” said Bolivia’s Minister of the Presidency, Fernando Aramayo.

The rapprochement comes at a time of alignment between the two governments, which this year joined the Shield of the Americas, the US-backed regional security alliance. The Bolivian opposition, however, criticised the visit over the destruction in Chile of part of a seized shipment of Bolivian timber over alleged traces of drugs. “The situation is tense, we cannot be hypocrites,” said deputy Elena Pachacute of the Unidad alliance.

#18. Lula accuses Bolsonaro of “licking Trump’s boots” in the final debate

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday accused his runoff rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, of “licking the boots” of US President Donald Trump during the last televised debate before Sunday’s election.

Lula said Bolsonaro was behind Trump’s decision to impose tariffs on Brazilian imports, a recurring accusation the senator has repeatedly denied. “But I wasn’t worried; if Trump doesn’t want to buy from Brazil, I’ll sell elsewhere,” he said in the TV Globo debate, referring to the opening of new markets during his term. Lula replied that his rival “memorises but doesn’t learn” and that agriculture received more resources under his government than under former president Jair Bolsonaro, the candidate’s father.

Bolsonaro won the first round with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%, and the latest Datafolha poll puts them level at 50% of valid votes each.

#19. Milei calls Lula a “leftist thief” and says he hopes he will not “steal” Brazil’s election

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Argentine President Javier Milei attacked his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva again on Tuesday, accusing him of a “dirty campaign” and saying he hoped Lula would not try to “steal” Sunday’s presidential runoff, in which he faces Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, whom Milei has publicly backed.

“Progressive male chauvinists… Then they go around accusing all their opponents of misogyny… The mask is slipping on these criminals… I hope his latest dirty campaign trick doesn’t include stealing the election… Leftist thief,” Milei wrote on X. The message was accompanied by a clip from a television interview in which Lula defended the shorter working week, approved last week by the Senate, arguing that “a woman cannot work six days a week and rest one, because on that day she has to clean the house”.

It is not the first time Milei has called Lula a “thief”. On October 7 he posted an image of the Brazilian president with that word on Instagram, and in July he called him a “jailbird” and a “thief”, prompting Brazil to recall its ambassador in Buenos Aires for consultations, according to the EFE news agency. Lula was convicted of corruption in the Lava Jato investigation and spent 580 days in prison, but the Supreme Federal Court annulled his convictions in 2021, restoring his political rights. The Brazilian government had not commented on the new message.

On Sunday, in the first runoff debate, Lula asked Bolsonaro whether he intends to apply “Milei’s chainsaw” to cut public spending. Bolsonaro won the first round with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%, and polls show a statistical tie.

Brazil is Argentina’s main trading partner, and the two countries are Mercosur’s largest economies.

#20. Pressure mounts on Paraguay’s Central Bank over doubts about some lenders’ solvency

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

The Association of Banks of Paraguay, which groups 14 private lenders, on Sunday asked the Central Bank of Paraguay to report on the solvency of institutions that received facilities in merger processes, days after senators from the ruling party and the opposition called on President Santiago Peña to remove the institution’s leadership.

“We ask the Central Bank to report on the solvency of all entities that received facilities in merger processes. That way doubts will be cleared and, if any entity does not comply, action can be taken in time,” the association said in a statement released by local media. It added that the soundness of lenders cannot rest on “differential treatment”.

The request comes after the Central Bank reported to the Senate, at its request, on the conduct of several private lenders, including Ueno Bank, which according to local media has attracted substantial public deposits in just a few years. The association considers that report “incomplete” and says concern persists over the credit exposure of a private bank, which it does not identify, to companies in its own group.

On Wednesday, senators from several parties urged Peña to dismiss the Central Bank’s board, and in particular its president, Carlos Carvallo. Days earlier, the president had publicly backed the institution and called for calm amid rumours about Ueno Bank. Neither the Central Bank nor the lender has commented on the association’s statement.

In 2024, Peña described as a “media campaign” and “lies” reports on the purchase by the Social Security Institute of 250 billion guaraníes in Ueno Bank bonds. The bank’s head, Juan Manuel Gustale, said at the time that Peña was a shareholder in Ueno Holding and not in the bank, and the president said in April 2025 that he had sold those shares.

#21. US lifts sanctions on Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

The US Treasury Department on Wednesday removed from its sanctions list Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly and brother of acting president Delcy Rodríguez. The Treasury did not explain the reasons for the decision.

Rodríguez, who has led the Venezuelan parliament since 2021, was taken off the Office of Foreign Assets Control’s Specially Designated Nationals list, which entails the blocking of assets in the United States, a ban on entering the country and a prohibition on transactions with US citizens and companies. He had been designated in September 2018, along with his sister, former first lady Cilia Flores and then defence minister Vladimir Padrino. At the time, the Treasury said Nicolás Maduro had given them “high-ranking positions” in the government to help him “remain in power”.

Rodríguez was removed from the list in April, which allowed her to travel to New York in September for the UN General Assembly, where she met US President Donald Trump. Rodríguez took power after Maduro and Flores were detained in a US military operation in Caracas in January; both face charges in New York of drug trafficking and, since last week, of torture and repression.

Since then, the Rodríguez government has negotiated an oil agreement with Washington, announced in August, which according to El País gives the United States majority control over a fifth of Venezuela’s reserves, the largest in the world. According to Reuters, the Rodríguez siblings pushed legal changes to further open the energy and mining sectors to foreign companies.

Presidential elections remain without a date. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio received in Washington Dinorah Figuera, head of the opposition delegation in talks with the Venezuelan government, with no announcements. Opposition leader María Corina Machado is not taking part in that dialogue and has been unable to return to Venezuela.

#24. The Pope cancels a visit to Assisi as a medical precaution, two weeks before his South American tour

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Pope Leo XIV has cancelled a visit planned for Tuesday, October 27, to Assisi, in central Italy, after his doctors advised against helicopter travel so soon after the lung surgery he underwent on October 13. It is the first engagement on his schedule to be called off since the operation, two weeks before the start of his tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

According to a medical bulletin released by the Vatican on Friday, a follow-up chest X-ray “confirmed his optimal post-operative recovery”. “However, given the short time that has elapsed since surgery, the attending physicians considered it appropriate to advise against the helicopter flight planned for October 27 as a precautionary measure,” it added.

In Assisi, the Pope was due to take part in a peace gathering marking the 40th anniversary of the World Day of Prayer for Peace convened by John Paul II. He will send a message to the organisers and participants.

Leo XIV, 71, underwent surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, where he was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma. On Wednesday, the Vatican said the tumour was localised and that he will not need further treatment. On Sunday, in his first appearance before the faithful since the operation, the Pope said he would resume his activities “gradually”.

The Vatican has announced no changes to the South American tour, scheduled from November 6 to 17, which will begin in Uruguay, from the 6th to the 8th, and continue in Argentina, until the 11th, and in Peru.

#25. Lubetkin warns Flávio Bolsonaro that “it is not easy to leave Mercosur”

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Uruguay’s Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin has warned Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro that “it is not easy to leave Mercosur”, in response to his criticism of the bloc during the campaign for the October 25 runoff. In the same interview, with the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, he said Uruguay would not restore diplomatic relations with Venezuela while Delcy Rodríguez governs.

“It is not easy to leave Mercosur. There are too many interrelated agreements in the business sphere, and that would cause major losses for the Brazilian economy. And there are too many mechanisms that prevent such a quick exit,” Lubetkin said. “I hope that, if that gentleman ends up presiding over Brazil, when he starts governing he will realise that many statements made during the election campaign are impracticable once in government.”

The government programme Bolsonaro registered with the Superior Electoral Court does not mention Mercosur. On the campaign trail, the senator has spoken of “freeing Brazil from the shackles of Mercosur”, referring to the constraints the common external tariff places on negotiating its own trade agreements, a phrase some media have interpreted as raising the possibility of leaving the bloc. Uruguay has held the Mercosur pro tempore presidency since July 1.

Lubetkin said Uruguay would work with whoever is elected: “First, let the elections be clean, transparent, democratic and calm. Then, naturally, the Brazilian people will choose whoever they consider best, and we will work with whoever wins, as state policy.”

On Venezuela, the minister ruled out resuming relations: “In no way, and we are not going to resume them.” He argued that from elections Uruguay had questioned “came a president who is now, on top of everything, imprisoned in the United States, and from that president comes a president as illegitimate as he was”. Uruguay will restore ties, he said, when “an independent court confirms” the winner of a democratic election. Caracas withdrew its diplomatic staff from Uruguay and six other Latin American countries in July 2024 after they questioned Nicolás Maduro’s re-election; Maduro has been detained in the United States since January. Rodríguez announced at the UN in September that elections would be held, without setting a date.

#27. Iguazú Falls closed as the river’s flow tops 12,000 cubic metres per second

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Iguazú National Park, in Argentina’s Misiones province, closed access to the falls’ walkways on Monday because of an exceptional rise in the Iguazú River, whose flow exceeded 12,000 cubic metres per second. The flood is part of an episode of heavy rainfall linked to El Niño that has also caused the Uruguay River to burst its banks, with evacuations on both sides.

According to the Argentine Naval Prefecture, the river rose just over two metres between Sunday and Monday at Puerto Iguazú and reached a level of 24.30 metres, and was still rising. The alert level is 25 metres and the evacuation level 28. The park authority and the concessionaire halted ticket sales during Monday’s public holiday and inspected trails and infrastructure, where some small trees fell. “We may be able to open normally tomorrow,” park authorities told the newspaper La Nación. The flood had been forecast weeks in advance by the National Parks Administration.

Cierre total en las Cataratas del Iguazú por crecida histórica Las intensas y extraordinarias lluvias registradas en las cuencas de los ríos Paraná e Iguazú obligaron a las autoridades a cerrar de manera preventiva el acceso al público en el Parque Nacional Iguazú. De acuerdo con las autoridades, el flujo de agua superó los 12.000 metros cúbicos por segundo, lo que representa casi 10 veces el volumen normal de los saltos. Imágenes : Tiempo_AMBA en X y lucasdiaz.birding en Instagram

Rain in the upper basin, in southern Brazil, has also swollen the Uruguay River. In Uruguay, the first families were evacuated in Salto on October 10, and the departmental emergency committee has gone into permanent session. In Paysandú, the river reached 6.25 metres on Sunday, close to the evacuation level of 6.89, and 35 people had to leave their homes, some housed in army tents. The ferry service between Monte Caseros and Bella Unión was suspended.

On the Argentine side, seven families were evacuated in Concordia, where the river is expected to stay around 11.60 metres until Thursday, and 31 people in Paso de los Libres. The binational Salto Grande dam is releasing about 18,000 cubic metres per second.

Forecasts place the current El Niño among the most intense in recent decades. Last week, an atmospheric river intensified by the same phenomenon brought Santiago, Chile, its wettest October on record and a mudslide in the Las Condes district.

#30. Lula and Bolsonaro agree to open their bank and phone records days before the runoff

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro signed an agreement at the Superior Electoral Court on Thursday to simultaneously lift the secrecy of their bank, tax and phone records, and those of relatives and linked companies, three days before Sunday’s presidential runoff. Release of the data now depends on a decision by Judge André Mendonça, the case rapporteur.

The document covers the past eight years and provides for the information, requested from the Central Bank, financial institutions, the tax authority and phone companies, to be published on a public portal of the electoral courts. Lula signed in person; Bolsonaro did so through his lawyer, Maria Claudia Bucchianeri, who had sought to extend the period covered. Allies of the president expressed doubts about whether the senator would comply.

The initiative arose from a challenge Lula issued to his rival during Sunday’s televised debate. On Tuesday, the president filed authorisation with the court to open his data if Bolsonaro did the same. The senator made his acceptance conditional on including presidential corporate card spending since 2023, the schedule of First Lady Janja Lula da Silva, visits by the president’s children to the official residence, the use of official helicopters and the government’s links with former banker Daniel Vorcaro. Lula’s campaign accepted the conditions, according to its coordinator, Senator Camilo Santana.

The agreement comes amid mutual accusations of corruption. Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering in connection with the Banco Master case, and one of the president’s sons, Fábio Luís Lula da Silva, for alleged influence peddling. Both deny the accusations.

Polls show a statistical tie between the two candidates, who hold their final debate on Friday on TV Globo.

#32. Operativos de Fuerzas Armadas dejan detenidos en Guayaquil y Esmeraldas

Esmeraldas y Guayas son provincias que actualmente se encuentran bajo estado de excepción.

El despliegue de las Fuerzas Armadas dejó detenidos y un duro golpe a estructuras criminales, en las últimas horas, en Guayas y Esmeraldas.

En sus redes sociales, las FF. AA. informaron sobre los operativos militares realizados en Guayaquil y Esmeraldas, así como sus resultados.

En Guayaquil, por ejemplo, las Fuerzas Armadas, a través de la Fuerza de Tarea Conjunta Guayas, ejecutaron una operación de ámbito interno en el sector Vergeles. Durante la intervención, fue aprehendido alias Chupón. La institución compartió imágenes de esta detención, con armas y celulares decomisados.

En la misma ciudad, la Fuerza de Tarea Conjunta destruyó un inmueble presuntamente vinculado al grupo de delincuencia organizada (GDO) Los Fatales. Las FF. AA. informaron que el operativo se realizó en Flor de Bastión, donde se decomisaron celulares, armas blancas y otros elementos.

A la vez, en el sector de Sauces 4, uniformados aprehendieron a una ciudadana conocida como alias la China, presuntamente vinculada a Los Tiguerones.

Por otro lado, en Esmeraldas, las Fuerzas Armadas indicaron que, a través de la Armada, ejecutaron operaciones militares en el redondel de Tachina. Durante la intervención, el personal naval interceptó una motocicleta en la que se movilizaban dos ciudadanos, en cuyo poder se encontró un arma y celulares.

En la misma provincia, en el sector Cabo San Francisco, en el cantón Muisne, los militares encontraron varios paquetes con sustancias catalogadas sujetas a fiscalización.

En sus publicaciones en la cuenta de X, las FF. AA. compartieron imágenes con las detenciones y los elementos decomisados tras estos operativos.

Esmeraldas y Guayas, junto con El Oro, Los Ríos, Manabí, Pichincha, Santa Elena y Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas, son provincias que actualmente se encuentran en estado de excepción, decretado por el presidente Daniel Noboa el pasado 15 de septiembre. En tanto, desde el 1 hasta el 10 de noviembre entrará en vigencia el toque de queda focalizado para las provincias de Guayas, Esmeraldas, Manabí, Los Ríos y El Oro, de 00:00 a 05:00. (I)

#34. US confirms concern over the impact of Argentina’s Falklands bill on its companies

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau acknowledged in Buenos Aires on Thursday that Washington is closely watching the impact that Argentina’s National Sovereignty Defence bill, which toughens sanctions against those involved in hydrocarbon exploitation in the Falklands, could have on its companies. Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno defended the initiative.

“We are obviously looking at the interests of our companies. It is natural for any country to be concerned about that, but I want to stress that we respect the legislative process of the great Argentine nation,” Landau said at a joint press conference at the San Martín Palace, after meeting Quirno together with Assistant Secretary for Western Hemisphere Affairs Juan Pablo Segura. The US concern centres on the bill’s extension of sanctions to affiliates, shareholders, financiers and suppliers of the companies involved, as the newspaper Clarín reported on Sunday.

Quirno said current legislation needs changes to give the country better tools and denied that the bill targets anyone in particular: “This law is not against anyone in particular, it is not against any company in particular.” He explained that it seeks to make companies choose between investing on the mainland or in the islands. “We hope they will always choose the Argentine mainland over the illegitimate licences of the Malvinas Islands,” he said. The bill remains stalled in the Chamber of Deputies.

Landau also defended the US proposal to end the UN Decolonisation Committee, before which Argentina presents its claim every year, as part of a broader reform of multilateral bodies, and asked that it not be read in light of any specific dispute. Quirno replied that its possible disappearance would not weaken Argentina’s claim or UN resolutions: “Our claim is global, in every international forum and above all at the United Nations.” He reiterated that Argentina seeks a peaceful negotiation with the United Kingdom.

On bilateral matters, Quirno announced US funding against drug trafficking and child trafficking and for a cybersecurity centre, and a framework with the Export-Import Bank to explore up to US$7 billion in financing for the Andes-Atlantic Corridor. On the conditions of Washington’s support, he said: “The only condition is that we keep doing what we are doing.” US Vice President JD Vance is expected to visit Argentina in November.

#35. Scientific workshop on Illex Squid in Vigo with the participation of Falkland Islands

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Argentine unions linked to the fishing, maritime and port industries have complained bitterly to the International Transport Workers Federation against a workshop on the Shortfin Squid (Illex Argentinus) organized by OPPC3, in Vigo with the suppot of the Sustaianble Fisheries Partnership, and to which Argentina allegedly has not been invited, but it does include the Falkland Islands.

OPPC3 stands for Organization of Producers of Freezer Trawlers for Hake, Cephalopods and Other Species. OPPC3 is based in Vigo, was started in 1986 when Spain joined the EU and represents approximately 60% of the European Union's freezer vessel fleet specializing in species like hake and squid.

The workshop with scientists from Brazil, Uruguay, the Falkland Islands, Spain, China and South Korea participating, aims to build a regional database and update scientific knowledge in order to assess the abundance and exploitation status of Argentine shortfin squid (Illex argentinus), which supports the largest fishery by landed volume in the South Atlantic Ocean.

Under the name of 4th International Scientific Workshop on Argentine shortfin squid (Illex argentinus) the event brought together scientists specializing in fisheries biology, population dynamics and stock assessment from the above mentioned countires.

The workshop aim was to continue advancing the development of a shared regional database and improve scientific knowledge of the abundance, productivity and exploitation status of this species.

The initiative is organized and funded by the Organization of Producers of Freezer Trawlers for Hake, Cephalopods and Other Species (OPPC3), with facilitation support from Sustainable Fisheries Partnership (SFP).

The workshop forms part of an international scientific cooperation process that began with meetings held in Chile and Panama and continued with a scientific gathering in Bangkok. The Vigo meeting represented a new step forward in strengthening collaboration between scientists and representatives of the fleets harvesting Illex argentinus throughout the Southwest Atlantic.

The fishery operates across waters shared by multiple nations and fishing fleets, in a context where no fully operational regional governance framework currently exists to coordinate stock assessment and resource management. Against this backdrop, the workshop seeks to foster greater cooperation among stakeholders by encouraging the exchange of scientific and fisheries information that can help reduce uncertainty regarding the status of the stock.

According to Edelmiro Ulloa, Managing Director of OPPC3, collaboration is essential to ensuring the long-term sustainability of the fishery: “The sustainability of a shared fishery requires the fleets operating on the resource to work together to improve the information available. Reducing uncertainty benefits companies, workers, administrations and scientists alike, while contributing to more responsible, predictable and sustainable management of the resource.” OPPC3 believes that scientific cooperation and information exchange should be viewed as an opportunity to strengthen the health of the fishery and safeguard the economic activity and employment that depend upon it.

The workshop was scientifically chaired by Rubén Roa-Ureta, an independent expert in statistical modelling and fisheries stock assessment who has supported the initiative since its earliest stages.

According to Roa-Ureta, Illex argentinus is a species of enormous ecological, economic and social importance for the countries, industries and communities that depend on it. As a result, obtaining the best possible scientific assessment of its status and dynamics is a shared priority.

The work carried out in Vigo is expected to help consolidate a common technical foundation for future assessments, improve understanding of population dynamics and identify the key uncertainties that still need to be addressed.

Maybe the organisers see Argentina as a difficult and disruptive partner and unlikely to work together, share information and reach consensus. They only have themselves to blame for exclusion.

#39. Paraguay's opposition takes Asunción from the Colorado Party and holds Ciudad del Este

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Paraguay's opposition won the mayoralty of Asunción and held that of Ciudad del Este, the country's two most populous cities, in Sunday's municipal elections, according to preliminary results from the electoral authority. The ruling Colorado Party, however, won the vast majority of districts.

With 99.92% of polling stations counted, civil engineer Soledad Núñez of the Alianza Juntos por Asunción won 47.78% of the vote to 45.98% for Colorado candidate Camilo Pérez, president of the Paraguayan Olympic Committee, a margin of 5,024 votes. Núñez was backed by the Patria Querida and Authentic Radical Liberal parties. “Asunción voted, Asunción won. Today the people who don't give up, who resist, who can't be bought, won,” she said on election night.

In Ciudad del Este, Daniel Pereira Mujica of the opposition Yo Creo party won with 72.83%, keeping the city in the hands of the party previously led locally by Miguel Prieto. Prieto has expressed interest in running for president in 2028.

The Colorado Party, to which President Santiago Peña belongs, was winning in 187 of 263 districts and 11 of 17 departmental capitals, and regained the mayoralty of Encarnación. The figures from the preliminary results transmission system must be confirmed by the official count.

After the vote, Núñez said the opposition would file a complaint with prosecutors over the publication of exit polls during election day. A consultancy posted trends for several cities on social media an hour before polls closed, without naming candidates. The Electoral Code prohibits publishing such polls until an hour after closing. “This goes against electoral participation,” said Núñez, who argued the publication may have discouraged voters. Liberal senator Celeste Amarilla called the poll “illegal” and said she would file a complaint if no one else did. The consultancy was not publicly identified and did not comment. Turnout in Asunción was 61.75%, up from 59.65% in 2021.

Municipal elections serve as a political barometer ahead of the 2028 general election.

For Argentina, Fund economist Petya Koeva Brooks attributed the 1.4-point cut to “lower activity observed through the third quarter of this year” and to “weaker domestic demand in a context of still tight domestic financial conditions and the continued structural transformation of the economy”. The Fund also raised its forecast for average inflation this year to 32.5%, from 30.4% in April, and for 2027 to 21.2%, from 15.7%. It projects unemployment of 7.6% in 2026 and 7.1% in 2027. Argentina’s growth forecast for next year was revised from 4% to 3.5%. Economy Minister Luis Caputo is attending the meetings.

Uruguay’s forecast was cut by half a point to 1.3%, in line with the Fund mission that visited the country in September, which attributed the slowdown to the impact of drought on farming. Chile saw the largest adjustment, of 1.8 points. Brazil would grow 2.2% this year and 1.9% in 2027, two and three tenths less than in July, because of still-tight monetary conditions and the withdrawal of fiscal support. For the region, the Fund expects 2.5% growth in 2027 and inflation of 6.8% this year, excluding Venezuela. According to the report, higher energy prices benefit commodity exporters and hurt importers.

Globally, the Fund forecasts growth of 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, while global inflation would rise to 4.7% this year, driven by energy and food. It assumes an average oil price of US$95.74 a barrel in 2026, against US$67.74 in 2025, and that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027.

In the United States, headline inflation would rise to 3.6% this year and fall to 2.8% in 2027, while the economy would grow 2.3% in both years, supported by consumption, fiscal policy and investment in artificial intelligence. The Fund identifies a prolonged war in the Middle East and an abrupt correction in expectations about artificial intelligence as the main risks.

#43. Trump won’t betray Britain over the Falklands

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

By Nile Gardiner (*) - In his second term, Donald Trump has aggressively pursued an America First foreign policy. And rightly so. The U.S. president represents the American people, and every policy he advances should be in his nation’s interest. But backing British sovereignty over the Falkland Islands fits firmly within this vision, and his administration should stand shoulder to shoulder with the UK on an issue of huge importance to the British people.

Last month, in response to questions from British media, President Trump declared that the U.S. would review its long-standing policy of neutrality on the Falklands issue. This was immediately seized upon by Argentina’s president Javier Milei, a close ally of Trump, who announced tougher sanctions against foreign companies with plans to drill for oil around the Falkland Islands, as well as a renewed push to end British sovereignty.

The U.S. president has also seemed to equivocate over the question of whether the U.S. would come to Britain’s aid in the event of a future war between London and Buenos Aires. Trump made it clear he was hugely disappointed in the refusal of the British Government to back U.S. military action against Iran.

Trump Will Never Forgive Burnham if the Chagos Deal Is Resurrected Having worked closely with the U.S. administration in opposition to Labor’s disastrous Chagos surrender deal, I have witnessed first-hand the White House’s immense frustration with Britain’s socialist government, which has frequently been at odds with Trump’s team, from the Iran war and Israel to net zero, mass migration and freedom of speech. The Trump administration has been particularly unhappy over Labour dragging its feet on a firm commitment to swiftly increase defence spending in line with Nato commitments made at the Hague summit last year.

This is the tensest relationship that I have seen between London and Washington in nearly a quarter of a century in the D.C. policy world. The reality is that Labour simply isn’t trusted, and the renewed push on Chagos by No 10 under Andy Burnham on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly further underscored this. The British Government has been acting as its own worst enemy.

But I do not believe the Trump presidency will ultimately shift the U.S. position on the Falklands, despite all the stupid actions of the Labour Government. Here’s why.

The Anglo-American special relationship still matters inside the Washington Beltway, in both the executive branch and on Capitol Hill. The King’s visit to the U.S. in April was a stunning success, with even “No Kings” Democrat Members of Congress giving King Charles a series of standing ovations when he spoke to a joint session of Congress.

President Trump’s extremely warm reception for the King at the White House and his speech welcoming the King at the arrival ceremony, which I attended, were a glowing tribute to the enduring strength of our two great nations. The bottom line is that President Trump loves Britain, the British people and his British heritage through his Scottish mother. And like Trump, nearly 60 million Americans have British ancestry according to the 2020 census, including much of America’s political and economic leadership.

How the U.S.-Europe Rift Got Balkanized Throw into the mix the massive levels of trade and investment between the two countries, the vital strategic importance of the U.S./UK base at Diego Garcia, the key role played by RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire (despite the decision to temporarily remove U.S. stealth strategic bombers in the wake of an Iranian terror plot), and the extremely close intelligence ties between the CIA and MI6, and the special relationship remains very real.

Not a single American official I have spoken with in the last few months has told me they support a change in U.S. policy over the Falklands. They understand the huge importance this issue has to the British people, and all of them speak of their admiration for Margaret Thatcher who ordered the liberation of the islands from Argentina following the brutal invasion by its military junta in 1982.

U.S. officials also acknowledge that the Argentine position over the Falklands was viewed sympathetically by the Obama administration when Hillary Clinton was Secretary of State and far-Left Cristina Kirchner was Argentina’s president. Republicans are reluctant to take a stance that Democrats have traditionally favored in Washington, and which would be championed by the American Left.

There remains immense goodwill in the United States towards Great Britain and the British people, and very little desire to throw America’s closest ally under the bus over the Falklands. It is firmly in the U.S. national interest to defend the vital principles of sovereignty and self-determination the American people cherish. This piece originally appeared in The Telegraph.

(*) Nile Gardiner is Director of The Heritage Foundation’s Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom and Bernard and Barbara Lomas Fellow.

#46. Uruguay ranks third in Latin America for international air passengers per capita

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

Uruguay ranked third in Latin America and the Caribbean in 2025 for international air passengers per inhabitant, according to Airports Council International figures presented in Lima this week, despite its small share of the region's total traffic.

The country recorded 0.67 international passengers per inhabitant, behind only the Dominican Republic, at 1.71, and Costa Rica, at 1.62. As an outside reference, the United States recorded 0.77. Argentina, by contrast, stood at 0.34.

Absolute volume tells a different story. Uruguay's airports handled some 2.3 million passengers in 2025, compared with 235 million in Brazil, 191 million in Mexico, 100 million in Colombia and 50 million in Argentina. In total passengers per inhabitant, Uruguay recorded 0.68, below most of the region's large markets and above Paraguay, Ecuador, Guatemala and Honduras, among others.

The director general of the organisation's Latin American branch, ACI-LAC, Rafael Echevarne, attributed Uruguay's position to the development of Carrasco International Airport and its integration with logistics activity. “Uruguay is one of the star countries, not only in the region but almost worldwide,” he told the newspaper El País. He highlighted the Latin America Cargo City logistics centre at Carrasco, which he said has become a regional hub for the pharmaceutical industry serving Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay, as well as the integration between the airport and the port of Montevideo. The airport and its logistics centre are operated by the Corporación América group.

The figures come against a regional market growing at a more moderate pace. In the first half of 2026, passenger traffic in Latin America and the Caribbean rose 1.9% and cargo 3.6%. ACI-LAC projects long-term growth of 3.1% a year, taking the region from some 809 million passengers this year to around 1.5 billion in 2045, with required investment estimated at US$178 billion over thirty years.

The post-pandemic recovery has been uneven: according to the organisation, 133 airports in the region remain below their 2019 passenger traffic and 161 have not recovered their cargo levels.

#48. The US waives beef tariffs for Brazil and Paraguay, but not for Argentina and Uruguay

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

US President Donald Trump signed a proclamation on August 26 temporarily waiving tariffs on imports of up to 300,000 tonnes of lean beef trimmings, a measure that excludes countries already holding their own quotas in the US market, among them Argentina and Uruguay. The main beneficiaries will be Brazil and Paraguay.

The text, titled Further Ensuring Affordable Beef for the American Consumer, invokes section 404 of the Uruguay Round Agreements Act, which allows a president to widen a tariff-rate quota temporarily. The expansion will run for 90 days from September 1, with a maximum of 100,000 tonnes a month allocated on a first-come, first-served basis in three tranches until November 30.

The exclusion stems from a technical point. The proclamation allocates the entire additional volume to the statistical category of “other countries or areas,” which does not include exporters holding country-specific quotas. That leaves out Argentina, Uruguay, Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, which obtained its own 13,000-tonne allocation on January 1, as well as Canada and Mexico, covered by the free trade agreement.

For Brazil, the largest beef supplier to the US market, the measure removes for three months the out-of-quota duty of 26.4% it has paid since mid-January. Paraguay qualifies through the same channel: it shipped 23,497 tonnes in January, though it has since remained below 5,000 tonnes a month.

Argentina holds its own quota, historically 20,000 tonnes a year, which a proclamation on February 6 raised to 100,000 for this calendar year. Mario Ravettino, president of the ABC Export Consortium, confirmed the country is excluded along with Uruguay, Australia and New Zealand, and that the only beneficiary would be Brazil. “We are analysing it,” he told the newspaper La Nación.

The scale of the loss is debatable. Colin Carter, professor emeritus of agricultural economics at the University of California, Davis, said Argentina is not currently a significant supplier of the product covered by the programme, lean trimmings intended to be blended with US beef to make ground beef. In Brazil, the exporters' association Abiec said its members could benefit, though the requirement to sell those cuts at a discount of around 25% limits margin gains.

The White House justified the decision on the decline of the US cattle herd, which it places at its lowest level in 75 years, and on restrictions on live cattle imports from Mexico over the New World screwworm, drought and wildfires. The Department of Agriculture projects production will fall by around 4% compared with 2025. Trump warned he could revoke the measure to prevent a windfall for foreign producers if the discount does not materialise.

#50. A magnitude 7.7 earthquake shakes Panama

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:44 UTC

A magnitude 7.7 earthquake shook Panama on Friday at 12:56 local time, centred on the Azuero peninsula in Herrera province, according to the US Geological Survey. Panamanian authorities have not so far confirmed any casualties, though inspections are continuing and they have not ruled out injuries or people trapped. Damage to buildings was reported in several provinces.

The epicentre was about 14 kilometres southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, a sparsely populated area near the Pacific coast some 240 kilometres from the capital, at shallow depth. Panama’s Institute of Geosciences estimated the magnitude at 7.2. Its director, Néstor Luque, attributed the quake to the Azuero-Sona fault system, which had been accumulating stress for some time. More than 30 aftershocks were recorded.

The National Civil Protection System reported damage in Penonomé, in Coclé province, including to the cathedral of San Juan Bautista, the governor’s office and a hotel, as well as in Chitré and Venao. Its director, Omar Smith, warned that aftershocks would continue, though with decreasing intensity.

The Education Ministry cancelled afternoon classes nationwide, public offices were closed, water supply was cut in some areas because of power failures and Tocumen international airport temporarily suspended operations. The Panama Canal Authority said the waterway was operating normally.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center issued an alert for the coasts of Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador and Mexico, which was lifted hours later. Smith had considered a tsunami unlikely because the epicentre was on land. In Chile, the navy declared a precautionary alert for Easter Island and lifted it after the magnitude, initially estimated at 8.0, was revised. The quake was felt in the Colombian cities of Medellín and Cartagena.

President José Raúl Mulino called for calm and asked emergency agencies for a report on the effects. “What has happened must not be used to generate alarm and disorder,” he wrote.

The earthquake comes two months after a magnitude 7.4 quake that killed 335 people in Colombia’s Chocó department on August 10.

#51. Juezas Daniella Camacho e Inés Romero están descalificadas del concurso público para elegir al fiscal de Ecuador

Consejeros de mayoría del CPCCS ratificaron la eliminación de varios exaspirantes en la etapa de impugnación y escrutinio público.

El Consejo de Participación Ciudadana y Control Social (CPCCS) dejó en firme la descalificación de Daniella Camacho, del concurso público de designación del titular de la Fiscalía General del Estado.

Este 23 de octubre de 2026, el pleno del CPCCS fue convocado para resolver más de 20 solicitudes de apelación a las resoluciones emitidas por la comisión ciudadana —encargada de desarrollar el concurso público para la elección del fiscal general— que descalificó a 21 participantes, de los 26 que estaban en la carrera, en la fase de impugnación ciudadana.

La sesión virtual, que se instaló con casi dos horas de retraso, confirmó la descalificación de la postulante Daniella Camacho, actual jueza de la Corte Nacional de Justicia (CNJ) y quien encabezaba la lista de los mejor puntuados con 48/50 en la calificación de sus méritos.

Los informes no vinculantes para resolución del pleno, fueron elaborados por Cristina Tamayo Jaramillo, abogada de la Coordinación Jurídica, quien recomendó ratificar las resoluciones emitidas por la comisión ciudadana con las que se descalificó a las 21 personas. Entre estas, a Camacho, porque no cuentan —a criterio de las autoridades— con probidad e idoneidad para ejercer este cargo.

La eliminación de Camacho del concurso se resolvió con el voto de los consejeros y candidatos a la reelección en el CPCCS, Andrés Fantoni, Johanna Verdezoto, Jazmín Enríquez, Johnny Escobar; y, el nuevo vocal Andrés Mendoza, quien se principalizó en lugar de David Rosero, destituido por juicio político.

Se abstuvo de votar Piedad Cuarán y también Nicole Bonifaz.

Esta última consejera fundamentó que, por respeto al debido proceso no se pronunciaría sobre las causas relacionadas con Camacho, ya que ella, en su rol de jueza nacional, dictó auto de llamamiento a juicio en el caso Ligados en el que Bonifaz es procesada.

En todo caso, la funcionaria Cristina Tamayo sugirió aceptar la apelación presentada por el abogado Patricio Rosero, quien impugnó a Daniella Camacho.

Él esgrimió que la jueza se excusó de ser parte de los tribunales de juicio en contra de Wilman Terán, exjuez nacional y expresidente del Consejo de la Judicatura (CJ), cuando este fue sentenciado por delincuencia organizada en el denominado caso Metástasis.

Efectivamente, la jueza admitió que se apartó de despachar esa causa, porque tenía una “amistad íntima” —figura contemplada en el Código Orgánico Integral Penal— con Terán. Pese a que la magistrada alegó que su decisión de apartarse cumplía con las disposiciones legales, fue excluida del proceso.

Los consejeros de mayoría rechazaron también las apelaciones que presentaron la misma Daniella Camacho, quien fue descalificada por la comisión; Inés Romero, jueza de la Corte Provincial de Justicia de Pichincha y de Walter Macías, exjuez nacional, por lo que están eliminados del concurso.

Por ahora, los cinco concursantes que continúan fijos en la competencia son:

En esta plenaria, también se conocieron recusaciones planteadas en contra de la consejera Nicole Bonifaz y de Fantoni y Verdezoto.

La recusante es la ciudadana Mónica Jaramillo —que impugnó a la exaspirante Inés Romero—, quien pidió que se instale una audiencia para resolver su recusación en contra de Fantoni y Verdezoto, por lo que el tratamiento de los casos relacionados con Romero no se tratarían.

Está previsto que se instale un nuevo pleno extraordinario este sábado (24 de octubre) a las 16:30 para resolver las recusaciones en contra de Fantoni y Verdezoto.

Jaramillo también recusó a Bonifaz, pero el pleno rechazó el pedido.

Luego de que el CPCCS se pronuncie sobre las apelaciones, los concursantes que sigan en la competencia enfrentarán la última etapa del proceso, como es la prueba escrita y la exposición de un caso práctico relacionado con las funciones de la Fiscalía.

El examen escrito está valorado sobre 30 puntos y el oral 20/50, que se sumarán a los 50 puntos que hayan obtenido en méritos.

Aquel postulante que en la suma alcance la nota más alta deberá ser designada por el CPCCS como titular de la Fiscalía General para un periodo de seis años. (I)

By Vicky Kapogianni Associate Professor of International and Environmental Law, University of Reading - Argentina is trying to stop a planned oil project near the Falkland Islands. On October 13, the government asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Seas (Itlos), a court in Hamburg that deals with disputes over the sea, to halt the project. Argentina says the UK approved the drilling without its agreement and in breach of Argentina’s rights to the seabed.

The project, called Sea Lion, is a joint venture between UK and Israeli companies, and has been licensed to produce oil by the Falkland Islands government. The Sea Lion field holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil, 500 million barrels of which is assessed as recoverable.

Argentina began arbitration proceedings against the UK on September 28 and gave London 14 days to stop the project. That deadline expired on October 12. The Argentine government has now called on Itlos to issue “provisional measures” – emergency orders to protect each side’s rights, or prevent serious harm to the marine environment.

The UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has rejected Argentina’s claims, insisting the UK will “vigorously” contest jurisdiction.

Itlos applies the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which governs the sea – not land. Yet rights at sea flow from owning the coast, which means that whoever holds the Falklands holds the seabed – and the oil – around the Islands. Tribunals under the convention have no power to decide who owns land, and can’t settle sovereignty disputes.

Because rights at sea flow from land, every question about the oil in the dispute between Argentina and the UK has been dragged back into a near two-century argument over who owns the Islands.

We proposed settling boundaries, resources and environmental protection on the basis of fairness, as Australia and Timor-Leste agreed in 2018 to share revenue from oil and gas in the Timor Sea.

Argentina’s request asks Itlos to order the UK to prevent Sea Lion from starting production while the arbitration is under way. The Argentine government warns that commencing extraction would create an “irreversible fait accompli”.

To back its argument, Argentina is relying on a 2015 order in a sea-border dispute between Ghana and Ivory Coast. There, the tribunal allowed Ghana’s existing oil operations to continue but banned new drilling. So the question is whether – with Sea Lion’s development due to begin in early 2027 – the project could be halted in the same way.

The tribunal must also accept that the rights at stake are “plausible” – meaning there is a credible legal basis for them, even though the full case has yet to be heard. For Ivory Coast, this was simple. Nobody disputed that both countries had coastlines over which they had sovereignty. The only argument was over where the sea border between them should run.

For Argentina, it is an uphill battle. It insists it is not seeking a ruling on sovereignty, yet its request rests on “sovereign rights” over the continental shelf. It is hard to judge that this is a plausible claim without asking who owns the Islands.

In April, a tribunal hearing a dispute between Ukraine and Russian over coastal rights in the Black Sea close to the occupied Ukrainian province of Crimea found that Russia had breached the convention over the Kerch Strait bridge, which connects Russia with Crimea along with associated power cables and gas pipelines. Ukraine had brought the case in 2016, two years after Russia annexed Crimea, accusing it of usurping Ukraine’s rights in the surrounding waters – from drilling rigs to shipping lanes – and seeking compensation.

The tribunal found that Russia’s environmental assessments were inadequate and unpublished, and that it failed to cooperate in protecting the marine environment.

How could the tribunal say all this without deciding who owns Crimea? Because duties such as assessing environmental impact apply to activities under a state’s “jurisdiction or control”. What mattered was that Russia controlled the bridge, cables and gas pipelines. Who owns Crimea could be left for another day.

Could the same reasoning apply to Sea Lion? The UK answers for the Islands internationally, and the convention requires states to ensure that activities under their jurisdiction or control do not cause pollution damage to other states. Argentina’s request cites a spill contingency plan by Premier Oil, Sea Lion’s former operator, which put the chance that oil from a blowout would cross into Argentine waters after 30 days at 30%. A tribunal could, without having to determine who owns the oil, consider whether the UK has assessed and shared such risks.

The tribunal relating to Crimea held that the award was “appropriate declaratory relief”. This meant its formal, binding finding that Russia had broken the law was the sole remedy. Russia was not ordered to change its conduct or pay reparation for its environmental breaches.

So what are Argentina’s chances of success if it pursues an argument about the project’s environmental risk? Real, but the victory, if it comes, may not stop Sea Lion going ahead, and it won’t determine Argentina’s ownership of the Falkland Islands.

Even an interim order requiring the UK to assess and share the project’s environmental risks with Argentina would represent a win of sorts.

And with an election next year in which the incumbent president, Javier Milei, is struggling, and given how strongly most Argentines feel about the issued, even a modest win could help the president.

Any order for Argentina and the UK to cooperate would bring London and Buenos Aires back to the same table over Sea Lion. A conversation about shared risks could be the first step towards sharing the resources.

Airports in Latin America and the Caribbean will require investment of around US$178 billion over the next thirty years to handle demand that would rise from 809 million passengers this year to around 1.5 billion in 2045, according to projections presented in Lima at the annual assembly of Airports Council International.

The director general of the organisation's regional branch, ACI-LAC, Rafael Echevarne, estimated long-term growth of 3.1% a year and said annual infrastructure spending would need to rise from about US$3.4 billion to between US$8.6 and 8.7 billion by mid-century. Globally, ACI estimates the sector will need around US$4.6 trillion in investment through 2055, after a record 9.8 billion passengers in 2025 and 4.7 billion in the first half of this year. “What really matters now is how we make sure our industry is ready for this growth,” said ACI World director general Justin Erbacci.

Echevarne warned that connectivity within the region has not recovered since the pandemic. “We have lost 20% of the city pairs we had connected,” he said, placing the loss mainly at regional airports in Peru, Ecuador and Chile. He put forward liberalisation of air transport as the main tool to reverse it: “We need to move from signing treaties of good intentions to putting that opening into practice.”

The organisation also argued that airport charges, set by each country's regulators rather than by the airports themselves, account for a small share of airline costs. According to IATA figures cited at the meeting, they represent 4.3% of operating costs globally and 5.5% in the region when air traffic control fees are included. The average charge is around US$9 per passenger.

Brazil leads regional traffic with 235 million passengers in 2025, followed by Mexico with 191 million, Colombia with 100, Argentina with 50, Peru with 43 and Chile with 36. In international trips per inhabitant, Uruguay ranks third among the Latin American countries surveyed, at 0.67, behind the Dominican Republic and Costa Rica, and nearly double Argentina's 0.34. Panama leads in total traffic per inhabitant, at 4.59.

In Argentina, the government on Monday formalised the extension to 2049 of the concession for 35 airports held by Aeropuertos Argentina, part of the Corporación América group, with an option to extend to 2056. #69. Uruguay ranks third in Latin America for international air passengers per capita

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:45 UTC

Uruguay ranked third in Latin America and the Caribbean in 2025 for international air passengers per inhabitant, according to Airports Council International figures presented in Lima this week, despite its small share of the region's total traffic.

The country recorded 0.67 international passengers per inhabitant, behind only the Dominican Republic, at 1.71, and Costa Rica, at 1.62. As an outside reference, the United States recorded 0.77. Argentina, by contrast, stood at 0.34.

Absolute volume tells a different story. Uruguay's airports handled some 2.3 million passengers in 2025, compared with 235 million in Brazil, 191 million in Mexico, 100 million in Colombia and 50 million in Argentina. In total passengers per inhabitant, Uruguay recorded 0.68, below most of the region's large markets and above Paraguay, Ecuador, Guatemala and Honduras, among others.

The director general of the organisation's Latin American branch, ACI-LAC, Rafael Echevarne, attributed Uruguay's position to the development of Carrasco International Airport and its integration with logistics activity. “Uruguay is one of the star countries, not only in the region but almost worldwide,” he told the newspaper El País. He highlighted the Latin America Cargo City logistics centre at Carrasco, which he said has become a regional hub for the pharmaceutical industry serving Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay, as well as the integration between the airport and the port of Montevideo. The airport and its logistics centre are operated by the Corporación América group.

The figures come against a regional market growing at a more moderate pace. In the first half of 2026, passenger traffic in Latin America and the Caribbean rose 1.9% and cargo 3.6%. ACI-LAC projects long-term growth of 3.1% a year, taking the region from some 809 million passengers this year to around 1.5 billion in 2045, with required investment estimated at US$178 billion over thirty years.

The post-pandemic recovery has been uneven: according to the organisation, 133 airports in the region remain below their 2019 passenger traffic and 161 have not recovered their cargo levels.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva invoked the War of the Triple Alliance (1864-1870) to defend increased defense spending, in remarks that drew formal rejection this week from both chambers of Paraguay's Congress.

During a visit on Friday to a plant belonging to the defense company Avibras Aeroespacial, Lula said Brazil likes peace but cannot forget that Paraguay one day decided to invade Brazil, adding that it later did the same to Argentina and Uruguay. Press accounts differ on the order in which he named the three countries.

Paraguay's Senate approved a declaration on Wednesday, in an extraordinary session, to strongly condemn the remarks. The text, proposed by opposition senator Eduardo Nakayama, argues that the comments distort and unilaterally simplify the origins of the conflict and cast Paraguay as the sole aggressor, omitting the Brazilian Empire's intervention in Uruguay. Senators urged Brazilian authorities to adopt a respectful, balanced and truthful treatment of the two countries' shared history, and stressed that Paraguay poses no threat to Brazil's sovereignty or territorial integrity.

The Chamber of Deputies approved a declaration along similar lines by majority vote and added a request that Santiago Peña's government pursue diplomatic efforts toward the return of war trophies still held in Brazil. Among them it cited the Cristiano Cannon, an artillery piece cast in 1866 from bronze church bells donated by the population and now held at the National Historical Museum in Rio de Janeiro.

Paraguayan lawmakers and historians maintain that the conflict did not stem from expansionist ambitions on their country's part but as a response by the Paraguayan government of the day to Brazil's military intervention in Uruguay's civil war in 1864. The origins of the war remain a subject of historiographical debate.

Estimates of Paraguay's human losses vary widely and no academic consensus exists, given the absence of reliable census records. Paraguay's foreign ministry has issued no official statement, a silence criticized by lawmakers across party lines. Nakayama attributed the remarks to electoral calculation on Lula's part, an interpretation the senator himself presented as conjecture. Brazil holds general elections in October.

#73. Amazon fires rise 62% in October as deforestation falls to a record low

Montevideo, October 25th 2026 - 05:45 UTC

Satellites detected 9,045 fire hotspots in the Brazilian Amazon in the first half of October, 62% more than in the same period last year, amid a drought aggravated by El Niño. The increase contrasts with the fall in deforestation, which over the past year reached its lowest level since 1988.

The situation is particularly serious around Manaus, the capital of Amazonas state, home to more than two million people, which has been covered in smoke for weeks with air quality among the worst in the world. On Saturday, civil defence sent a “severe alert” to residents’ mobile phones urging them to stay at home, and classes were suspended at some schools. The federal government deployed more than 300 firefighters and 11 aircraft to support the fire services.

According to Ane Alencar, director of science at the Amazon Environmental Research Institute, most of the fires are set deliberately, generally to clear land for cattle, and the drought has turned the forest into a tinderbox. Alencar noted that September was the second month with the fewest fires on record and that the situation changed after the first round of the presidential election on October 4, and suggested as a hypothesis that the expectation of a change of government may have played a role: “I think the prevailing thought is ‘we won’t be punished’.” The head of the federal environment agency Ibama, Jair Schmitt, told the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo that the police and the intelligence agency are investigating whether there is “something orchestrated and structured”.

Between August 2025 and July 2026, 3,355 square kilometres of the Amazon were deforested, 42% less than in the previous period and the lowest figure since 1988, against 11,600 square kilometres in 2022. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s government has set a target of zero deforestation by 2030.

The campaign of opposition candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who faces Lula in Sunday’s runoff, has used the smoke to criticise the government’s record. His programme proposes eliminating illegal deforestation by 2029 using artificial intelligence and satellite imagery. He has not responded to the researcher’s hypothesis.
